case.background: Monochromatic light illuminates a clean cathode in a vacuum phototube. Vary frequency and the absorbed photon rate, then use stopping potential and saturation current to explain when and how electrons are emitted.
initial_observations: Some illumination settings produce no measurable photocurrent.
When electrons are emitted, a reverse voltage can stop the current.

controls.description: Absorbed photon rate at the cathode relative to the reference setting.
controls.name: absorbed_photon_flux_relative

instruments.description: A clean-cathode vacuum phototube with monochromatic illumination and electrical meters.
instruments.name: vacuum_phototube

notes: The cathode remains clean and unchanged across experiments.
When a work function is reported in volts, it denotes the energy divided by elementary charge.
The photon-flux control is absorbed photon rate, not optical power or irradiance.
Above threshold, the ideal cathode has frequency-independent quantum yield and the saturation circuit collects every emitted electron.
Zero current and stopping potential mean no emitted electrons.

No candidate law family or truth-specific parameter slots are supplied.

readouts.description: Reverse-potential magnitude needed to reduce photocurrent to zero.
readouts.name: stopping_potential_v

readouts.description: Saturation photocurrent with all emitted electrons collected.
readouts.name: saturation_current_ua
